title: Fitting a preprocessing scaler
prompt: A preprocessing scaler is being fitted for a new model. Which practices are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Include the test data when fitting the scaler because labels are not used.
options.explanation: Even without labels, the test inputs would influence the fitted statistics (mean, min, max, ...), which leaks information about the test set into training and makes the evaluation optimistic. The test set must stay unseen until the final evaluation.

options.text: Normalizing only the training data while leaving validation and test inputs unnormalized creates a preprocessing mismatch.
options.explanation: The network learns on inputs with the normalized scale, so unnormalized validation or test inputs live on a different scale and the learned weights no longer behave as expected. Every split must go through the same transform.

options.text: Reuse those fitted statistics on validation, test, and future inputs.
options.explanation: The scaler is part of the model: the statistics computed once on the training data must be applied unchanged at validation, test and deployment time so that inputs are on the scale the network was trained on.

options.text: Fit its statistics on the training split only.
options.explanation: Fitting on the training split only keeps validation and test data truly unseen, so their scores are honest estimates of performance on new data.

hints: Think about what information the model is allowed to see before the final evaluation.
The scaler's statistics are learned from data, just like weights.
explanation: A scaler's statistics are learned from data, so they must be computed on the training split only (otherwise information leaks from the test set) and then frozen. The same frozen transform has to be applied to validation, test and future inputs, otherwise the model sees inputs on a different scale than the one it was trained on. The rule is: fit on train, transform everything with those statistics.

title: Min-max scaling to a custom range
prompt: A feature ranges from 10 to 30 in the fitting data. General min-max scaling maps this interval linearly to $[-1, 1]$. What is the transformed value of $x = 15$? Give the answer to 2 decimals.
hints: First map the value to $[0, 1]$ with $(x - \min)/(\max - \min)$.
Then stretch to a range of width 2 and shift so that the minimum lands on -1.
explanation:
General min-max scaling to $[a, b]$ is

$$x' = a + \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}\,(b - a)$$

Here $x' = -1 + \frac{15 - 10}{30 - 10}\cdot 2 = -1 + 0.25\cdot 2 = -0.5$. Equivalently, 15 is a quarter of the way from 10 to 30, and a quarter of the way through $[-1, 1]$ is $-0.5$.

Common wrong results: 0.25 is the value for the standard $[0, 1]$ range (forgetting to stretch and shift to $[-1, 1]$); 0.5 is the value of the mirrored point 25, i.e. measuring from the wrong end of the range; -1 is the value of the minimum, 10, not of 15.

title: Counting depth of an MLP
prompt: An MLP has widths 10 -> 6 -> 4 -> 3. Count depth using affine layers only, excluding the input and counting the output layer. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: There are four hidden layers.
options.explanation: Four is the number of width entries in the list, which includes the input and the output. Hidden layers are only those strictly between input and output, here two.

options.text: There are three affine layers.
options.explanation: Each arrow between consecutive widths is one affine map: 10 -> 6, 6 -> 4 and 4 -> 3, so three affine layers, and the depth is 3.

options.text: There are two hidden layers, with widths 6 and 4.
options.explanation: The hidden layers are the layers between the input (width 10) and the output (width 3), namely the layers of width 6 and 4.

options.text: The output has width 10.
options.explanation: Width 10 is the input dimension. The output is the last entry of the list, so its width is 3.

hints: Draw the widths as a chain and count the arrows between them.
Which entries of the list are the input and the output?
explanation: With widths listed from input to output, the number of affine layers is the number of widths minus one, here 3. The first entry is the input, the last is the output, and everything in between (6 and 4) is hidden. Do not confuse the number of listed widths with the number of layers.

title: The symmetry problem in dense networks
prompt: In a standard dense MLP without neuron-specific randomness, all hidden units start with identical incoming weights, identical biases, and identical outgoing connections. Which statements describe the symmetry problem? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Different positions in a weight matrix automatically force different learned features.
options.explanation: Position in the matrix does not matter by itself: if the entries of two rows are equal, the corresponding neurons compute the same function and receive the same gradient. Only different initial values can make them diverge.

options.text: The hidden units initially compute the same function.
options.explanation: Identical incoming weights and biases give identical pre-activations and therefore identical outputs for every input.

options.text: Setting every weight to the same nonzero constant necessarily breaks the symmetry.
options.explanation: A nonzero constant makes the weights non-zero but still identical, so the symmetry is fully preserved. Breaking it requires different values per neuron, e.g. random initialization.

options.text: Under identical gradient updates, their parameters remain identical.
options.explanation: Identical units with identical outgoing connections receive identical gradients, so the same update is applied to each and they stay identical for the whole training.

hints: If two units have exactly the same parameters, can their gradients differ?
Is a constant nonzero value any different from a constant zero value regarding symmetry?
explanation: If hidden units share incoming weights, biases and outgoing weights, they compute the same output and get the same gradient, so gradient descent keeps them identical forever and the layer behaves like a single neuron. The fix is to break the symmetry with different (random) initial values per neuron; a constant initialization, zero or nonzero, never does that.

title: Standardizing a feature value
prompt: A feature has training mean 10 and training standard deviation 2. Ignoring epsilon, what is the standardized value of $x = 13$? Give the answer to 2 decimals.
hints: Subtract the training mean first.
Then divide by the standard deviation (not the variance).
explanation:
Standardization uses the training statistics:

$$z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{13 - 10}{2} = 1.5$$

The value is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

Common wrong results: 6.5 is $13/2$ (dividing without subtracting the mean); 0.75 is $(13 - 10)/4$ (dividing by the variance $\sigma^2 = 4$ instead of $\sigma$); 3 is $13 - 10$ (subtracting the mean but forgetting to divide).

title: Multiplying by an orthogonal matrix
prompt: $Q$ is a square real orthogonal matrix satisfying `Q.T @ Q = I`. Which statements about multiplication by $Q$ are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Norm preservation automatically remains exact after every nonlinear activation.
options.explanation: Only the linear map $x \mapsto Qx$ preserves the norm. A nonlinearity such as ReLU can change it: for $y = (1, -1)$ ReLU gives $(1, 0)$, whose norm is 1 instead of $\sqrt{2}$.

options.text: $Q$ must leave every coordinate of $x$ unchanged.
options.explanation: Orthogonal matrices include rotations, reflections and permutations, which change coordinates. A 90 degree rotation sends $(1, 0)$ to $(0, 1)$. Only the identity leaves every coordinate unchanged.

options.text: For every vector $x$, multiplying by $Q$ preserves its Euclidean norm.
options.explanation: $\|Qx\|^2 = x^\top Q^\top Q x = x^\top x = \|x\|^2$, so lengths are preserved for every $x$.

options.text: The columns of $Q$ must each sum to 1.
options.explanation: The columns of an orthogonal matrix are orthonormal (unit length and mutually perpendicular), which says nothing about their sums. For the rotation with columns $(0, 1)$ and $(-1, 0)$ the sums are 1 and -1, and the matrix $-I$ has column sums of -1.

hints: Expand $\|Qx\|^2$ as $(Qx)^\top(Qx)$.
Think of rotations and reflections as examples of orthogonal matrices.
explanation: The defining property $Q^\top Q = I$ gives $\|Qx\|^2 = x^\top Q^\top Q x = \|x\|^2$, so orthogonal matrices preserve Euclidean lengths (they are rotations/reflections, possibly combined with permutations). This is a property of the linear map only; it does not mean coordinates stay fixed, columns sum to anything specific, or that later nonlinearities keep the norm.

title: Variance added by scaled residual contributions
prompt: Suppose $N$ mutually uncorrelated, zero-mean residual contributions are also uncorrelated with an initial stream $x_0$. Each unscaled contribution has variance $v$. Scale each contribution by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$. What is the total variance added by the $N$ contributions? (Select one answer.)

options.text: $N \times v$
options.explanation: This is the total variance of the unscaled contributions. It grows linearly with $N$, which is exactly what the $\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$ scaling is meant to prevent.
Each scaled term has variance $\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right)^2 v = \frac{v}{N}$, and for uncorrelated terms the variances add, so $N \cdot \frac{v}{N} = v$.

options.text: $\sqrt{N} \times v$
options.explanation: This treats the scaling as acting on the variance linearly or mixes up standard deviation and variance. Variance scales with the square of the factor, so $\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$ becomes $\frac{1}{N}$, and summing $N$ terms gives $v$, not $\sqrt{N}\,v$.

options.text: $\frac{v}{N}$
options.explanation: This is the variance of a single scaled contribution, not of the sum of all $N$. The $N$ uncorrelated terms add their variances, bringing the total back to $v$.

hints: How does the variance of a random variable change when it is multiplied by a constant $c$?
Variances of uncorrelated variables add.
explanation: For a constant $c$, $\mathrm{Var}(cZ) = c^2\,\mathrm{Var}(Z)$, so each scaled contribution has variance $v/N$. Because the contributions are mutually uncorrelated, the variance of the sum is the sum of the variances: $N \cdot v/N = v$. The $\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$ factor therefore keeps the total added variance independent of the number of residual contributions.

title: Reading activation histograms of a tanh network
prompt: Before training a deep tanh network, you inspect activation histograms. Which interpretations are reasonable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Activations collapsing toward zero across depth can indicate an initialization scale that is too small.
options.explanation: If weights are too small, each layer shrinks the signal, so activations in deeper layers concentrate near zero and carry little information (and give tiny gradients).

options.text: Outputs concentrating near -1 and +1 indicate tanh saturation.
options.explanation: tanh is bounded by $\pm 1$; when pre-activations are large the outputs pile up at the extremes, where the derivative is almost zero.

options.text: Very small gradients indicate that training updates may become too weak for effective learning.
options.explanation: Parameter updates are proportional to the gradients, so vanishingly small gradients lead to extremely slow or stalled learning.

options.text: One acceptable histogram guarantees successful optimization and good generalization.
options.explanation: A healthy histogram at initialization is only a sanity check. It says nothing about the data, the learning rate or generalization, which depend on many other factors.

hints: What happens to the derivative of tanh at the extremes of its range?
Is a diagnostic at initialization a proof of anything about the end of training?
explanation: Histograms at initialization diagnose the scale of the signal: too small weights make activations collapse to zero, too large ones saturate tanh at $\pm 1$, and both situations produce tiny gradients that make learning slow. A good-looking histogram is necessary for healthy training but never sufficient: it does not guarantee optimization success or generalization.

title: Absorbing the bias into the weight matrix
prompt: Which statements about absorbing a bias into a weight matrix are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The appended input coordinate must be a new randomly sampled value for each example.
options.explanation: The appended coordinate is the fixed constant 1 for every example. If it varied, the extra column would no longer act as a constant offset.

options.text: Appending a constant 1 to an input vector allows the bias to be represented by an extra weight-matrix column.
options.explanation: With $\tilde{x} = [x;\,1]$ and $\tilde{W} = [W \;\; b]$ we get $\tilde{W}\tilde{x} = Wx + b$.

options.text: Absorbing a bias into the matrix preserves the number of trainable scalar parameters.
options.explanation: $W \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times D}$ plus $b \in \mathbb{R}^{K}$ gives $KD + K$ parameters, and $\tilde{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times (D+1)}$ has $K(D+1) = KD + K$ entries: nothing is gained or lost.

options.text: The augmented column contains the original bias values.
options.explanation: The extra column of $\tilde{W}$ multiplies the constant 1, so it contributes exactly $b$ to the output, meaning the column is $b$.

hints: Write $\tilde{W}\tilde{x}$ block by block and compare with $Wx + b$.
Count the entries of the augmented matrix.
explanation: The bias trick appends a constant 1 to the input and appends the bias vector as an extra column of the weight matrix, so $\tilde{W}\tilde{x} = Wx + b$. It is only a notational convenience: the same $K(D+1)$ scalars are trained, and the appended coordinate is always the fixed constant 1, never random.

title: PCA rotation versus PCA whitening
prompt: Assume centered data with a positive-definite covariance matrix, and exact arithmetic. Which statements distinguish full-dimensional PCA rotation from PCA whitening? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Whitening requires each pair of original features to be independent before the transform.
options.explanation: Whitening is meant to remove correlations, so it does not require them to be absent beforehand. Any data with a positive-definite covariance can be whitened (and independence is a stronger condition than the uncorrelatedness whitening produces).

options.text: Whitening additionally rescales principal components to unit variance.
options.explanation: After the PCA rotation, whitening divides each component $i$ by $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$, giving every component variance 1 and an identity covariance.

options.text: PCA rotation alone always makes every component variance equal to 1.
options.explanation: After rotation the component variances are the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ of the covariance matrix, which are generally different from each other and from 1. Equalizing them to 1 needs the extra rescaling step.

options.text: PCA rotation diagonalizes the covariance matrix.
options.explanation: Rotating onto the eigenvectors gives covariance $\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d)$, so the components are uncorrelated.

hints: What is the covariance matrix of the data after rotating onto the eigenvectors?
What extra operation turns that covariance into the identity?
explanation: PCA rotation expresses the data in the eigenvector basis of the covariance, which makes the covariance diagonal with the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$ on the diagonal. Whitening adds a per-component division by $\sqrt{\lambda_i}$, so the covariance becomes the identity. Rotation decorrelates; whitening decorrelates and equalizes the variances.

title: Chaining two linear layers
prompt: An input batch has shape `(B, 10)`. A model applies `nn.Linear(10, 6)`, followed directly by `nn.Linear(4, 3)`. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Changing the batch size B fixes the feature-dimension mismatch.
options.explanation: The batch dimension is independent of the layer sizes. The mismatch is in the feature dimension (6 produced vs 4 expected), which no batch size can change.

options.text: Replacing the second layer with `nn.Linear(6, 3)` fixes the feature-dimension mismatch.
options.explanation: The first layer outputs `(B, 6)`, so the next layer must have `in_features = 6`; `nn.Linear(6, 3)` then produces `(B, 3)`.

options.text: The two layers are already compatible because both are fully connected.
options.explanation: Being fully connected is not enough: `out_features` of one layer must equal `in_features` of the next. Here 6 does not equal 4, so PyTorch raises a shape error.

options.text: The first layer produces a tensor of shape `(B, 4)`.
options.explanation: `nn.Linear(10, 6)` maps 10 input features to 6 output features, so its output is `(B, 6)`. The 4 is the expected input size of the second layer.

hints: Write the shape after each layer.
`nn.Linear(in, out)` acts on the last dimension only.
explanation: `nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)` maps `(B, in_features)` to `(B, out_features)`, so consecutive layers must satisfy `out_features` of the first equal to `in_features` of the second. Here the first layer yields `(B, 6)` but the second expects 4 features, so the fix is to change the second layer to `nn.Linear(6, 3)`. The batch size never plays a role.

title: Why zero biases are acceptable
prompt: Why can zero bias initialization be reasonable even though initializing all weights of a standard multilayer network to zero is problematic? (Select one answer.)

options.text: Zero biases force every activation to stay zero for every input.
options.explanation: With zero biases the pre-activation is $Wx$, which is nonzero whenever the weights and the input are nonzero. Activations do not stay at zero, and that would not be desirable anyway.

options.text: Biases must always be random for gradients to exist.
options.explanation: Gradients with respect to weights and biases exist regardless of their value; biases do not need to be random to be trained.

options.text: Zero biases imply that every neuron has identical weight vectors.
options.explanation: Biases and weights are independent parameters. Zero biases say nothing about the weights, which can still differ across neurons.

options.text: Independently randomized weights can already break neuron symmetry.
options.explanation: Different random incoming weights make neurons compute different functions and receive different gradients, so the bias does not need to supply any symmetry breaking.

hints: What exactly must an initialization do to avoid the symmetry problem?
Which parameters carry the neuron-specific randomness?
explanation: The goal of random initialization is to make different neurons different. If the weights are drawn independently, neurons already differ, so starting all biases at zero keeps the symmetry broken while giving a simple, centered starting point. Zero weights, in contrast, make all neurons identical and (in the usual setting) kill the gradient signal flowing to earlier layers.

title: Parameters of a small MLP with a bias-free first layer
prompt: An MLP has widths 8 -> 5 -> 3. The first affine layer has no bias; the second has a bias. The intermediate ReLU has no parameters. How many trainable scalar parameters are there?
hints: A layer from $n$ to $m$ units has $n \cdot m$ weights.
Add biases only for the layer that has them.
explanation:
First layer (no bias): $8 \cdot 5 = 40$ weights. Second layer: $5 \cdot 3 = 15$ weights plus 3 biases $= 18$. ReLU has no parameters. Total: $40 + 18 = 58$.

Common wrong results: 55 forgets the 3 biases of the second layer; 63 wrongly gives the first layer 5 biases as well ($45 + 18$); 48 is not produced by a consistent counting rule (for example it appears when the 8 input units are added to the 40 first-layer weights instead of counting the second weight matrix).

title: Min-max scaler on an out-of-range test value
prompt: A min-max scaler (output range $[0, 1]$) is fitted with training minimum 2 and maximum 10. No clipping or epsilon is used. A test value is 14. What does the fitted scaler output? Give the answer to 2 decimals.
hints: Always use the training minimum and maximum, never the test value's own range.
Without clipping, nothing forces the output to stay inside $[0, 1]$.
explanation:
The fitted scaler applies the frozen training statistics:

$$x' = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}} = \frac{14 - 2}{10 - 2} = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5$$

Because the test value lies outside the training range and no clipping is used, the result is above 1; that is expected and not an error.

Common wrong results: 14 means no scaling was applied; 1 comes from clipping to the training maximum, which was explicitly not used; 0.5 would be the output for $x = 6$, i.e. a wrong subtraction or ratio.

title: Parameters of a 6-4-2 MLP
prompt: An MLP has widths 6 -> 4 -> 2. Each fully connected layer includes one bias per output neuron. The intervening ReLU has no trainable parameters. How many trainable scalar parameters does the MLP have?
hints: Count weights and biases separately for each layer.
A layer with $n$ inputs and $m$ outputs has $n \cdot m + m$ parameters.
explanation:
First layer: $6 \cdot 4 + 4 = 28$. Second layer: $4 \cdot 2 + 2 = 10$. ReLU adds nothing. Total: $28 + 10 = 38$.

Common wrong results: 32 counts weights only ($24 + 8$) and forgets the biases; 36 forgets the 2 biases of the output layer ($24 + 4 + 8$); 44 is not produced by a consistent counting rule (for example it appears when the 6 input units are added as if they were parameters).

title: Data preparation practices
prompt: Which practices are appropriate when preparing data for model training and evaluation? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Cache one randomly augmented version of every image and assume this still gives fresh augmentation each epoch.
options.explanation: A cached augmented image is the same in every epoch, so the model repeatedly sees one fixed variant and the augmentation randomness is lost. Random augmentation has to be sampled anew each time an example is loaded.

options.text: Pad variable-length sequences and provide masks that identify padding.
options.explanation: Batching needs equal lengths, so shorter sequences are padded; the mask tells the model and the loss which positions are real so padding does not influence results.

options.text: Use suitable label-preserving random augmentation for training and deterministic preprocessing for standard validation.
options.explanation: Augmentation that keeps the label valid increases data diversity during training, while validation must be deterministic so scores are reproducible and comparable across runs.

options.text: Cache deterministic preprocessing steps, while sampling fresh random training augmentations online.
options.explanation: Deterministic steps (decoding, resizing) give the same result each time, so caching them saves time; the random part is applied on the fly so each epoch gets new variants.

hints: Which preprocessing steps give the same output every time, and which do not?
What should validation data look like from run to run?
explanation: Cache what is deterministic and recompute what is random: caching a random augmentation freezes it and removes its benefit. Validation should use fixed preprocessing for reproducible metrics, and variable-length data needs padding plus masks so the padded positions are ignored.

title: Covariance of a two-sample data matrix
prompt:
A data matrix has two samples stored as rows:

$$X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$$

Compute its feature covariance matrix after subtracting each column mean. Use the population convention, dividing by $n = 2$. Which matrix is correct? (Select one answer.)

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The diagonal (variances 1 and 4) is right, but the off-diagonal is wrongly 0. The second feature is exactly twice the first, so the covariance is $\frac{1}{2}\left((-1)(-2) + (1)(2)\right) = 2$.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: This is the sum $X_c^\top X_c$ without dividing by $n = 2$. The population covariance is this matrix divided by 2.

options.text: $\frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: This divides by $n^2 = 4$ instead of $n = 2$, which would be a double normalization.

options.text: $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$
options.explanation: The column means are $(2, 4)$, the centered rows are $(-1, -2)$ and $(1, 2)$, so $X_c^\top X_c = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix}$ and dividing by 2 gives $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$.

hints: Subtract the mean of each column first; the means are 2 and 4.
With samples in rows, the covariance is $\frac{1}{n} X_c^\top X_c$.
explanation:
Column means are $(2, 4)$, so the centered data is

$$X_c = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$

With samples in rows and the population convention, $\Sigma = \frac{1}{n} X_c^\top X_c = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$. The second feature is exactly twice the first, so the covariance is rank one.

title: Robust scaling of a value
prompt: A feature has training median 20, first quartile 12, and third quartile 28. Ignoring epsilon, what is the robust-scaled value of $x = 36$?
hints: Robust scaling subtracts the median.
It divides by the interquartile range, which is $Q_3 - Q_1$.
explanation:
Robust scaling is

$$x' = \frac{x - \text{median}}{Q_3 - Q_1} = \frac{36 - 20}{28 - 12} = \frac{16}{16} = 1$$

Common wrong results: 1.8 is $36/20$ (dividing by the median instead of subtracting it and dividing by the IQR); 2 is $16/8$ (using half the IQR, or $28 - 20$, as the denominator); 16 is the numerator alone, i.e. forgetting to divide.

title: Max-abs scaling versus robust scaling
prompt: Which statements about max-abs scaling and robust scaling are correct? Assume the fitted denominators are nonzero. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Robust scaling is generally less sensitive to a few extreme values than min-max scaling.
options.explanation: Min-max uses the extremes (min and max) directly, so a single outlier stretches the scale. Robust scaling uses the median and quartiles, which barely move when a few points are extreme.

options.text: Robust scaling typically subtracts the median and divides by the interquartile range.
options.explanation: That is the standard definition: $(x - \text{median})/(Q_3 - Q_1)$.

options.text: Robust scaling guarantees every transformed value lies in [-1, 1].
options.explanation: Robust scaling has no bounding guarantee. A value far above $Q_3$ maps to a large number; with median 20 and IQR 16, $x = 100$ becomes 5.

options.text: Max-abs scaling preserves zero entries because it divides by a scale without subtracting a center.
options.explanation: Zero divided by a nonzero constant stays zero, so sparsity is preserved. Subtracting a center (as min-max or standardization do) would move zeros to non-zero values.

hints: Which statistics does each scaler compute from the data?
Does the scaler subtract anything before dividing?
explanation: Max-abs scaling divides by $\max|x|$ with no centering, so zeros stay zero and sparsity is kept. Robust scaling centers at the median and divides by the IQR, which makes it much less affected by outliers than min-max scaling, but it does not bound the output to a fixed interval.

title: What changes across inputs at inference
prompt: During inference with a fixed trained MLP, which quantities normally change from one input example to another? (Select one answer.)

options.text: The number of hidden units.
options.explanation: The architecture, including the width of each layer, is fixed once the network is built; it does not depend on the input.

options.text: The input values and intermediate activations.
options.explanation: Each example has its own input vector, and passing it through the fixed weights produces example-specific hidden activations and outputs.

options.text: The learned biases because each example needs its own bias vector.
options.explanation: Biases are learned parameters shared by all examples. They are frozen at inference, not recomputed per example.

options.text: The trained weights of every layer.
options.explanation: The weights are only changed by training updates. At inference they are fixed and every example is processed with the same weights.

hints: What is a parameter, and what is a data-dependent value?
Which quantities are updated only by the optimizer?
explanation: At inference the model is a fixed function: the architecture and all parameters (weights and biases) stay constant. What changes with each example are the data-dependent quantities, namely the input and every intermediate activation computed from it, plus the output.

title: Where should normalization statistics come from?
prompt: Explain why the statistics of a scaler (mean and standard deviation, or minimum and maximum, or median and quartiles) must be computed on the training split only and then reused unchanged on validation, test and deployment data. What goes wrong if they are fitted on all the data, or refitted separately on each split?
model_answer: The scaler's statistics are part of the learned model, so they must come from training data only. Fitting them on validation or test data leaks information about those sets into training and gives optimistic evaluation results. Refitting them on each split makes the same raw value map to different scaled values, so the network, trained on the training scale, receives inputs it has never seen. Fixed training statistics keep the transform identical at train and deployment time, even if a test value falls outside the training range.
key_points: Statistics are learned from data, so they belong to the model and must use training data only.
Fitting on test or validation data leaks information and inflates the evaluation.
Refitting per split gives inconsistent scales between training and evaluation.
The same frozen transform must be used in deployment; out-of-range values then simply map outside the usual interval.
hints: Think about what information the model may see before the final evaluation.
Could the same raw value become different scaled values under different statistics?
explanation: The key idea is that preprocessing is a trained component, just like the weights. A strong answer mentions both leakage (when test data influence the statistics) and mismatch (when each split is scaled with its own statistics). A common half-answer only mentions leakage and forgets the scale consistency at deployment, or claims that leakage does not matter because labels are not used, which ignores that the inputs themselves carry information about the test distribution.

title: Symmetry breaking at initialization
prompt: Explain why initializing all weights of a multilayer network to the same value (zero or any constant) prevents it from learning useful distinct features, yet initializing all biases to zero is usually fine.
model_answer: If all hidden units share identical incoming weights, biases and outgoing weights, they compute the same output and receive the same gradient, so every update keeps them identical and the layer behaves like a single unit. Random, independent initial weights make the units differ, so their gradients and updates differ and they can specialize. Once the weights already differ, the biases do not need to break any symmetry, so starting them at zero is fine.
key_points: Identical units produce identical outputs and identical gradients.
Identical updates keep the units identical throughout training, so the layer is effectively one unit.
Any constant weight initialization, not only zero, preserves the symmetry.
Random weights break the symmetry, so zero biases do not cause a problem.
hints: Compare the gradients received by two units with identical parameters.
Which parameters have to differ across neurons for the symmetry to be broken?
explanation: The central argument is that gradient descent is deterministic and treats identical units identically, so it cannot break a symmetry that is present at initialization; only randomness in the initial weights can. A frequent mistake is to think that only zero initialization is a problem, when any constant value has the same effect, or to believe that biases must also be random, when different weights already make the neurons distinct.

title: What batching does to an MLP
prompt: For an MLP made only of affine layers and elementwise ReLU activations, which statements about batching are correct?

options.text: Changing the batch size necessarily changes the number of output classes.
options.explanation: The number of output classes is fixed by the width of the last layer. The batch size only changes the leading dimension of the tensors, e.g. $(B, K)$ with $K$ classes for any $B$.

options.text: A batch of 32 samples requires 32 separately learned copies of the MLP.
options.explanation: There is one network, not one per sample. Batching just stacks the 32 samples into a matrix and pushes them through the same layers at once, which is mainly a speed and gradient-averaging device.

options.text: Each sample is processed using the same weight matrices and biases.
options.explanation: Row $i$ of the batch output is $\text{ReLU}(x_i W^\top + b)$ with the same $W$ and $b$ for every row, so all samples share the parameters.

options.text: Increasing the batch size does not increase the number of trainable parameters.
options.explanation: The parameter count depends only on layer widths (e.g. $mn + m$ per dense layer), never on how many samples are processed together.

explanation: A batch is just several inputs stacked along a new leading axis. The weights and biases are shared by every sample, so the parameter count and the output width are independent of the batch size. Only the activations' memory and compute grow with the batch size. Do not confuse the batch dimension, which is a data dimension, with anything that is learned.

title: Scalar-node versus tensor-node drawings
prompt: The same dense computation can be drawn using many scalar nodes or one tensor-valued node. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Both drawing styles can represent exactly the same set of learned weights.
options.explanation: A scalar-node picture has one edge weight per entry of $W$, and the tensor-node picture stores the same entries as one matrix. Nothing is lost or gained by the notation.

options.text: A tensor-valued node can summarize many scalar computations.
options.explanation: One node such as $y = Wx + b$ stands for $m$ dot products at once, so it compresses many scalar nodes into a single box.

options.text: Input and output variables must always be drawn as separate nodes rather than annotated on edges.
options.explanation: Drawing conventions are flexible: variables can be separate nodes or labels on the edges between operation nodes. Neither is required, and neither changes the model.

options.text: Changing the drawing style alone does not change the computed function.
options.explanation: A diagram is only a notation for the same equations. The function changes only if the operations, parameters or connections change.

explanation: A computational graph is a way of drawing a computation, and scalar-level and tensor-level drawings are two levels of detail of the same function. Tensor nodes are simply a compact notation for many scalar operations. How variables are labelled (node or edge) is a presentation choice. Only changing the actual operations or parameters changes the function.

title: The computational-graph view of a network
prompt: Which statements describe the computational-graph view of a neural network?

options.text: Every node must represent exactly one scalar neuron.
options.explanation: Nodes can be scalar operations, but frameworks usually use tensor-valued nodes such as a matrix multiplication or a whole convolution. There is no one-neuron-per-node rule.

options.text: A node can consume tensors and produce tensors.
options.explanation: Operations such as matmul, conv or ReLU take whole tensors as inputs and return tensors, which is exactly how PyTorch and similar frameworks build the graph.

options.text: Edges contain only learned weights and never carry intermediate activations.
options.explanation: In a computational graph the edges carry values flowing between operations, i.e. inputs and intermediate activations. The learned weights are parameters (inputs to the operation nodes), not the only content of the edges.

options.text: Learnable parameters must be drawn explicitly for the graph to represent the network.
options.explanation: Parameters may be left implicit inside an operation node (e.g. a node labelled 'Linear'). The graph still represents the same network.

explanation: A computational graph describes how data flows through operations. Its nodes are operations that act on tensors, and its edges carry the values (inputs, activations) from one operation to the next. How much detail is shown, such as scalar versus tensor nodes or explicit versus implicit parameters, is a drawing choice and does not change the network.

title: Axes for a per-channel mean
prompt: RGB training images are stored in a tensor of shape $(N, 3, H, W)$. You want one mean per channel, pooled over all images and pixels. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Reduce over the sample, height, and width axes.
options.explanation: Averaging over axes 0, 2 and 3 (e.g. `x.mean(dim=(0, 2, 3))`) leaves only the channel axis, so each channel is averaged over all $N \cdot H \cdot W$ values.

options.text: The resulting mean vector has length 3.
options.explanation: After removing $N$, $H$ and $W$, only the channel axis of size 3 remains, giving one mean for each of R, G and B.

options.text: A separate mean must be learned for every image at inference.
options.explanation: The mean is computed once from the training set and then reused unchanged for all test images. It is a fixed statistic, not a learned per-image quantity.

options.text: Reduce over only the channel axis to obtain the three means.
options.explanation: Reducing over the channel axis would remove the channels and leave an $(N, H, W)$ tensor. To get one mean per channel you must keep the channel axis and reduce all the others.

explanation: To get a statistic per channel you keep the channel axis and reduce over every other axis: samples, height and width. The result has shape $(3,)$. It is computed on the training set only and reused for validation and test images. The classic mistake is to reduce over the axis you want to keep.

title: Undoing target standardization
prompt: A regression target was standardized as $y_{norm}=\frac{y-100}{20}$. A model predicts $y_{norm}=1.5$. What prediction $y$ in the original units should be used when reporting the error?
hints: Solve the standardization formula for $y$.
Multiply by the scale first, then add back the shift.
explanation:
Invert $y_{norm} = \frac{y - 100}{20}$: $y = 20 \cdot y_{norm} + 100 = 20 \cdot 1.5 + 100 = 30 + 100 = 130$.

Typical wrong results: 30 comes from multiplying by 20 but forgetting to add the mean back; 101.5 comes from adding 100 but forgetting to multiply by the scale; 0.075 comes from dividing by 20 instead of multiplying. Errors must be reported in original units, so the inverse transform is applied to predictions before computing the error.

title: Duplicates and data splits
prompt: Which statements about duplicate removal are correct?

options.text: Deduplicating before splitting helps prevent copies of the same example from entering different splits.
options.explanation: If copies are removed first, an example cannot end up in both training and test sets by chance, so the test set stays truly unseen.

options.text: Matching raw-byte hashes will detect every resized or re-encoded copy of an image.
options.explanation: Resizing or re-encoding changes the bytes, so the hash changes too. Detecting such copies needs perceptual hashes or embedding similarity.

options.text: A raw-byte hash can identify byte-identical files but may miss re-encoded copies of the same image.
options.explanation: Identical files give identical hashes, but a JPEG re-save of the same picture produces different bytes and therefore a different hash.

options.text: Near-duplicates across training and test sets can inflate measured performance.
options.explanation: If the model has effectively seen the test example during training, it can answer by memorization, so test accuracy overestimates real generalization.

explanation: Duplicates and near-duplicates that straddle the train/test boundary leak information and make the test score optimistic, so deduplicate before splitting. Exact byte hashes are cheap but only catch byte-identical files. Visually identical but re-encoded or resized copies need similarity-based methods.

title: Affine map on a small vector
prompt:
For the column-vector input $x = (2, -1)$, let

$$W = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b = (1, 0).$$

What is the affine output $z = Wx + b$ before any further operation?

options.explanation: This is $x + b = (2 + 1, -1 + 0)$: the matrix multiplication was skipped and the bias was just added to the input.
This is $Wx = (1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot(-1),\ -1\cdot 2 + 1\cdot(-1)) = (0, -3)$ without the bias. The bias still has to be added.
$Wx = (0, -3)$ from the row-by-vector dot products, and adding $b = (1, 0)$ gives $(1, -3)$.
This is just the bias $b$; it ignores the $Wx$ term entirely.

explanation: Each entry of $Wx$ is the dot product of one row of $W$ with $x$: $1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot(-1) = 0$ and $(-1)\cdot 2 + 1\cdot(-1) = -3$. Then add the bias entry by entry: $(0 + 1, -3 + 0) = (1, -3)$. The usual mistakes are forgetting the bias or skipping the matrix product.

title: Mean and variance after scaling and shifting
prompt: Let $Z$ have mean 0 and variance 1, and let $W = 0.03\,Z + 0.1$. Give the mean and the variance of $W$ (decimals, up to 4 decimal places).
hints: Expectation is linear. What does adding a constant do to the variance?
Scaling a variable by $a$ scales its variance by $a^2$.
explanation:
Mean: $E[W] = 0.03\,E[Z] + 0.1 = 0.03\cdot 0 + 0.1 = 0.1$.

Variance: adding a constant does not change variance, and scaling by $a$ multiplies it by $a^2$, so $\text{Var}(W) = 0.03^2 \cdot 1 = 0.0009$.

Typical wrong results: variance 0.03 uses the scale factor, which is the standard deviation, instead of its square; mean 0 and variance 1 are the statistics of $Z$ itself, ignoring the transformation; mean 0.03 with variance 0.1 swaps the roles of scale and shift. This is exactly how a standard normal sample is turned into a normal initialization with a chosen standard deviation and mean.

title: Mean image versus mean color
prompt: For aligned RGB training images of shape $(N, 3, H, W)$, compare a mean image (average over samples only) with a mean color (average over samples and spatial positions). Which statements are correct?

options.text: Both methods must subtract a different mean for each test image, estimated from that image.
options.explanation: Both statistics are estimated once on the training set and the same values are subtracted from every test image. Estimating them per test image would not be the same preprocessing.

options.text: The mean image has only three entries, regardless of H and W.
options.explanation: Three entries describes the mean color. The mean image keeps the spatial axes, so it has $3HW$ entries.

options.text: The mean image has shape $(3, H, W)$.
options.explanation: Averaging over only the sample axis removes $N$ and keeps channels and pixel positions, leaving $(3, H, W)$.

options.text: The mean color has shape $(3,)$.
options.explanation: Averaging over samples, height and width leaves one value per channel, so the shape is $(3,)$.

explanation: The set of axes you average over decides the shape of the statistic. Averaging over samples only gives a mean image of shape $(3, H, W)$ and requires aligned images. Averaging over samples and pixels gives a mean color of shape $(3,)$. In both cases the statistics are computed on the training data and reused for any new image.

title: Accuracy versus recall on imbalanced data
prompt: A dataset has 990 negative and 10 positive examples. A classifier always predicts negative. Positive-class recall means the fraction of actual positive examples predicted positive. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Its accuracy is 99%.
options.explanation: All 990 negatives are classified correctly and all 10 positives are wrong, so accuracy is $990/1000 = 99\%$.

options.text: Its positive-class recall is 99%.
options.explanation: The 99% is the accuracy, which is dominated by the negative class. Recall counts only the positives, and none of them is found.

options.text: Its recall for the positive class is 0%.
options.explanation: Recall is true positives divided by actual positives, $0/10 = 0\%$, because the classifier never predicts positive.

options.text: The high accuracy alone proves the rare class is detected well.
options.explanation: This classifier has 99% accuracy yet detects no positives at all. On imbalanced data accuracy can be high for a useless model, so you must also look at per-class metrics.

explanation: With 99% negatives, predicting 'negative' always achieves 99% accuracy while finding none of the positives (recall 0). Accuracy hides failure on the rare class, so imbalanced problems should be judged with per-class recall, precision or similar metrics.

title: Parameters of a dense image classifier
prompt: A dense classifier takes flattened RGB images of size 8 by 12 and returns 6 class scores. It has one bias per class. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The total parameter count is $(8\cdot 12\cdot 3)\cdot 6 + 6 = 1734$.
options.explanation: $8\cdot 12\cdot 3 = 288$ inputs, $288\cdot 6 = 1728$ weights, plus 6 biases gives $1734$.

options.text: The bias vector has 6 trainable entries.
options.explanation: There is one bias per output class and there are 6 classes.

options.text: Each image supplies $8\cdot 12\cdot 3 = 288$ input features.
options.explanation: The flattened image has height $\times$ width $\times$ channels $= 8\cdot 12\cdot 3 = 288$ values.

options.text: Doubling the number of images doubles the number of trainable parameters.
options.explanation: The parameter count depends on the layer shape, not on the amount of data or the batch size. More images only mean more forward passes through the same 1734 parameters.

explanation: A dense layer from $n$ inputs to $m$ outputs has $mn + m$ parameters. Here $n = 8\cdot 12\cdot 3 = 288$ and $m = 6$, so $288\cdot 6 + 6 = 1734$. The number of images in the dataset or batch never enters the parameter count.

title: Splitting speech data for unseen speakers
prompt: A dataset contains many recordings from each speaker. The goal is evaluation on previously unseen speakers. Which split is most appropriate?

options.text: Put exact duplicate recordings in different splits to balance their sizes.
options.explanation: Duplicates in different splits leak test content into training, so the test score becomes optimistic. Duplicates should be removed or kept together, never spread across splits.

options.text: Keep all recordings of a speaker in a single split.
options.explanation: Then test speakers are never seen in training, so the test score estimates performance on new speakers, which is the stated goal.

options.text: Randomly split recordings so every speaker appears in every split.
options.explanation: This measures performance on speakers the model has already heard (speaker leakage), which does not answer the question about unseen speakers.

options.text: Select the test recordings using the model with the highest test accuracy.
options.explanation: Choosing the test set (or the model) by looking at test accuracy is test-set tuning and makes the reported number biased. The test split must be fixed independently of results.

explanation: The split has to mirror the deployment scenario. To evaluate on unseen speakers, the unit of splitting is the speaker (group splitting), not the recording. A random recording-level split lets the model learn speaker-specific characteristics and inflates the test score.

title: Basic properties of an MLP
prompt: Which statements correctly describe an MLP?

options.text: It typically alternates fully connected layers with nonlinear activations.
options.explanation: The nonlinearities between affine layers are what make the network more expressive than a single linear map.

options.text: A fully connected layer is also called a dense layer.
options.explanation: Fully connected, dense and (in PyTorch) linear layers all refer to $y = Wx + b$ where every output depends on every input.

options.text: It is a feedforward network.
options.explanation: Information flows from input to output through the layers without cycles or feedback connections.

options.text: It requires a different set of weights for each sample in a batch.
options.explanation: Weights are shared by all samples. Each sample is processed with the same parameters, which is what lets the model generalize to new inputs.

explanation: An MLP is a feedforward stack of dense (fully connected) layers separated by nonlinear activations. The parameters belong to the network, not to individual samples, so the same weights are applied to every sample in a batch.

title: Pretrained backbone and a new head
prompt: You load a pretrained backbone and attach a newly created classifier head. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Loading a checkpoint replaces the initialized parameter values for the layers loaded from it.
options.explanation: Models are first constructed with some initial values; loading the state dict then overwrites those values with the saved ones for every matching layer.

options.text: Reinitializing every layer after loading would overwrite the learned backbone weights.
options.explanation: Reinitialization resets parameters to fresh random values, which discards what the checkpoint provided and throws away the pretraining.

options.text: Loading pretrained weights is equivalent to keeping the original random initialization.
options.explanation: They are opposite: random initialization is an uninformed starting point, while pretrained weights already encode learned features. That difference is the reason to load them.

options.text: The new classifier needs initialization.
options.explanation: The new head has no saved weights, so it starts from its own (random) initialization and is then trained or fine-tuned.

explanation: A checkpoint overrides the initialization only for the layers it contains. Layers that are not in the checkpoint, like a new head, keep their fresh initialization and must be trained. Re-initializing the whole model after loading would erase the pretrained knowledge, so initialize first, then load, or initialize only the new parts.

title: Shapes of W and b
prompt: In column-vector notation $y = Wx + b$, $x$ has length 7 and $y$ has length 4. What are the shapes of $W$ and $b$?

options.text: $W$ has shape $(7,7)$ and $b$ has shape $(4,)$.
options.explanation: A $(7,7)$ matrix applied to a length-7 vector gives length 7, not 4, so the output size would not match.

options.text: $W$ has shape $(4,7)$ and $b$ has shape $(4,)$.
options.explanation: A $(4,7)$ matrix times a length-7 vector gives a length-4 vector, and the bias must have the output's length 4.

options.text: $W$ has shape $(4,4)$ and $b$ has shape $(7,)$.
options.explanation: A $(4,4)$ matrix cannot multiply a length-7 vector, and a bias of length 7 cannot be added to a length-4 output.

options.text: $W$ has shape $(7,4)$ and $b$ has shape $(7,)$.
options.explanation: A $(7,4)$ matrix would need a length-4 input and would produce length 7. This mixes up input and output sizes (and the row-vector convention).

explanation: With column vectors, $W \in \mathbb{R}^{\text{out}\times\text{in}}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^{\text{out}}$. The number of columns of $W$ must match the input length (7) and the number of rows gives the output length (4). The bias has one entry per output.

title: Tabular preprocessing practices
prompt: Which practices are appropriate for tabular preprocessing?

options.text: Fit a median-imputation value using the training split.
options.explanation: Statistics for preprocessing are estimated only from the training data and then applied unchanged to validation and test data, so no test information leaks in.

options.text: Use the test-set median to fill missing training values.
options.explanation: This lets test-set information influence training, which is data leakage. The median must come from the training split.

options.text: A binary missingness indicator can preserve information about which values were absent.
options.explanation: After imputation the filled value looks like a real one; an extra 0/1 column keeps the fact that it was missing, which can itself be predictive.

options.text: Categorical features can be represented by one-hot vectors or learned embeddings.
options.explanation: Both turn category labels into numeric vectors, either as fixed sparse indicators or as dense vectors learned during training.

explanation: Preprocessing statistics (medians, means, scalers) are fit on the training split only and then reused for the other splits. Missingness can carry information, so an indicator column is often added alongside imputation. Categorical variables must become numeric vectors through one-hot encoding or embeddings.

title: Counting dense-layer parameters
prompt: A dense layer has $n$ scalar inputs and $m$ scalar outputs, with a bias for every output. Which statements are correct?

options.text: The layer has $mn + m$ trainable scalar parameters.
options.explanation: There are $m \cdot n$ weights (one per input-output pair) plus $m$ biases.

options.text: The weight matrix has shape $(m, n)$ in the expression $y = Wx + b$ with column-vector $x$.
options.explanation: $W$ has $m$ rows (outputs) and $n$ columns (inputs) so that $Wx$ has length $m$.

options.text: Each output must depend on only one input.
options.explanation: In a dense layer every output is connected to all $n$ inputs. A one-to-one dependence would be a diagonal or elementwise map, not a fully connected layer.

options.text: Each output has $n$ weights and one bias.
options.explanation: Output $j$ computes $\sum_i W_{ji} x_i + b_j$, which uses $n$ weights and one bias.

explanation: For a dense layer, each of the $m$ outputs has $n$ weights and one bias, so the layer has $mn + m$ parameters, with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$. Every output is connected to every input; that full connectivity is why it is called fully connected.

title: Batched dense layer in PyTorch
prompt: `X` has shape $(B, 7)$, `W` has shape $(4, 7)$ and `b` has shape $(4,)$. Using PyTorch-style matrix multiplication and broadcasting, which expressions give the dense-layer output of shape $(B, 4)$?

options.text: `X @ W.T + b`
options.explanation: `W.T` has shape $(7, 4)$, so `X @ W.T` is $(B, 4)$, and `b` of shape $(4,)$ broadcasts across the rows.

options.text: `X @ W + b`
options.explanation: `X @ W` multiplies $(B,7)$ by $(4,7)$, whose inner dimensions 7 and 4 do not match, so it raises an error. The weight must be transposed first.

options.text: `X * W + b`
options.explanation: `*` is elementwise multiplication, not a matrix product. $(B,7)$ and $(4,7)$ do not even broadcast unless $B$ is 1 or 4, and the result would be $(\cdot, 7)$, not $(B, 4)$.

options.text: `X @ W.transpose(0, 1) + b`
options.explanation: `transpose(0, 1)` swaps the two axes of the matrix exactly like `.T`, giving $(7, 4)$ and the same result as the first expression.

explanation: With samples as rows, the batched version of $y = Wx + b$ is $Y = X W^\top + b$. The weight matrix of shape $(\text{out}, \text{in})$ must be transposed so that the inner dimensions agree, and the bias is broadcast over the batch. `*` is elementwise and never performs a matrix product.

title: Batch shapes through an MLP
prompt: A batch of 12 feature vectors passes through an MLP with widths 10 -> 6 -> 4 -> 3. What is the sequence of batch tensor shapes?

options.explanation: The batch axis stays at 12 while the feature axis takes the successive widths 10, 6, 4 and 3.
This treats the batch size as an output width and shifts the dimensions of each layer: the batch size 12 disappears after the first layer.
Here the batch and feature sizes are multiplied and flattened ($12\cdot 6 = 72$, etc.). Dense layers act on the feature axis only and keep the batch axis.
The batch axis and the feature axis are swapped after the first layer. With samples as rows, the batch size 12 must remain the first dimension.

explanation: Dense layers transform only the last (feature) dimension and leave the batch dimension untouched. A $(12, 10)$ input through layers of width 6, 4 and 3 gives $(12, 6)$, $(12, 4)$ and $(12, 3)$. Batch size is never a feature width, and the batch is never flattened into the features.

title: Truncated normal initialization bounds
prompt: A normal initialization with standard deviation $0.02$ is truncated at two standard deviations on either side of zero. What are the absolute truncation bounds?

options.explanation: These are the bounds at one standard deviation. The truncation here is at two standard deviations, i.e. twice as far.
Two standard deviations: $2 \cdot 0.02 = 0.04$, so the bounds are $\pm 0.04$.
This squares the standard deviation ($0.02^2 = 0.0004$, the variance) and ignores the factor 2. The bounds are expressed in units of the standard deviation, not the variance.
This gives the bounds in units of standard deviations (the number 2) rather than in absolute values. Multiply by $\sigma = 0.02$ to get absolute bounds.

explanation: Truncation at $\pm k$ standard deviations means the absolute bounds are $\pm k\sigma$. With $k = 2$ and $\sigma = 0.02$ the bounds are $\pm 0.04$. The common errors are mixing up standard deviation and variance, or stating the bounds in units of $\sigma$ instead of absolute values.

title: Why batch size does not change the model
prompt: A dense layer with $n$ inputs and $m$ outputs is applied to a batch of $B$ samples stacked in a matrix $X$ of shape $(B, n)$. Explain why the number of trainable parameters and the output width do not depend on $B$, and write the shapes in the batched formula for the layer.
model_answer: The parameters of a dense layer are the weight matrix of shape $(m, n)$ and the bias of shape $(m,)$, which gives $mn + m$ values that depend only on the layer widths. All samples are processed with this same $W$ and $b$: the batched computation is $Y = X W^\top + b$ with shapes $(B, n)\,(n, m) \to (B, m)$, and the bias is broadcast over the rows. $B$ only appears as the leading, data-dependent dimension of the activations, so it changes memory and compute but not the model.
key_points: Parameter count is $mn + m$, determined only by the layer widths.
The same $W$ and $b$ are shared by every sample in the batch.
Batched form $Y = XW^\top + b$ with shapes $(B,n)$, $(n,m)$ giving $(B,m)$, bias broadcast over rows.
The batch size is only a data dimension and affects memory and compute, not the function class.
hints: Which tensors are learned, and which tensors are data?
What changes in the output shape when $B$ doubles?
explanation: The central idea is the distinction between parameters (shared, learned, fixed size) and data (a leading batch axis that can be any size). Common half-answers only say that 'batching is faster' or forget that the weights are shared, imagining a copy of the network per sample. Others write $XW$ without the transpose, which only works if $W$ is stored as $(n, m)$. A complete answer states the parameter count and the shapes of the batched formula.

source.item: Extra: leakage in splits and preprocessing

title: Keeping test information out of training
prompt: Explain why (a) duplicates must not be spread across train and test, (b) a dataset with many recordings per speaker should be split by speaker when the goal is to handle new speakers, and (c) imputation values and normalization statistics must be computed from the training split only. What do these three have in common?
model_answer: In each case, information about the test examples reaches the model through the training pipeline, so the test score measures memorization or familiarity instead of generalization to new data. Copies or near-copies of an example in both splits let the model recall the answer, recordings of the same speaker in both splits let it exploit speaker-specific traits, and computing a median or mean on the test data lets test values influence training inputs. To get an honest estimate, split first at the level that matches deployment (the speaker, the unique item), and fit all preprocessing on the training split only, applying it unchanged to validation and test data.
key_points: Identifies the common problem: leakage of test information into training makes the test score optimistic.
Duplicates or near-duplicates in both splits allow memorization rather than generalization.
Splitting by speaker (group) mirrors the deployment goal of unseen speakers; a random recording split does not.
Preprocessing statistics such as medians and means are fit on the training split and only applied to validation and test data.
hints: Ask what the model has effectively already seen when it is evaluated.
At which unit (recording, speaker, item) will the model be used in practice?
explanation: All three cases are forms of data leakage: the evaluation no longer reflects behaviour on truly new data. A weak answer lists the three practices without naming the shared cause, or says leakage only matters for duplicates. A strong answer connects each practice to what the test set is supposed to represent and states that the split is made first and preprocessing is fit afterwards.
